sessions.topic: Gas kiln workshop aftermath, Callum's Portugal move becomes concrete, Nadia's firing method shift

turns.message: okay so here's the thing, I need to tell you all about that gas reduction workshop I did last weekend and I cannot stop thinking about it. it was two days at a studio in the hills -- a proper anagama-adjacent setup, not the electric stuff we do here. the results are completely different. you cannot control it the same way and it took me until about hour six to stop fighting that and just let the kiln do what it does. I came home with pieces that look genuinely alive in a way my electric kiln work just doesn't. I think I need to seriously reconsider how I'm approaching my firing. 🔥

planted_challenges.fact_value: Nadia shifted from electric kiln preference to gas reduction kiln after attending a workshop
planted_challenges.evidence_span: You cannot control it the same way and it took me until about hour six to stop fighting that and just let the kiln do what it does. I came home with pieces that look genuinely alive in a way my electric kiln work just doesn't.

turns.message: Reduction atmosphere does something to iron glazes that electric simply cannot replicate. Technically speaking, the carbon in the flame affects the iron oxide at peak temperature -- you get the colour shifts, the metallic surfaces. I did a gas firing about four years ago and it changed how I think about surface. Not practical for weekly work but worth it occasionally.
wait oh my god the pieces you brought photos of look incredible
can I post one?? the matte grey on that tall one has the most amazing vibes
I'd rather you didn't, they're not finished -- I want to do some additional surface work before anything goes online. hold off for now. 🙏

That sounds like a significant experience, Nadia. I have always appreciated the consistency of the electric kiln -- for functional work the predictability matters because I'm making a matched set and variation between pieces creates problems. But I can see why the unpredictability would appeal for decorative work.
Unpredictable is not the same as uncontrolled. Gas reduction can be very precise.

Callum's right that matched sets need consistency. Technically speaking, that's exactly why porcelain in reduction is quite difficult -- you'd need to load the kiln identically each firing to get anything close to repeatable. Fair enough as a constraint.

planted_challenges.fact_value: Reuben understands that Callum prioritises functional consistency for matched sets over aesthetic exploration

Assuming we get everything sorted before the move, I want to finish a set of twelve matching dinner plates -- a proper send-off project. I am in phase one of the plate set: throwing and trimming all twelve to the same profile. Phase two will be glaze testing in the spring.

that's a brilliant project -- twelve matched plates is ambitious in porcelain. I'm going to miss having you here but if you're going to leave us you might as well go out with something properly done. I'll help with the glaze testing phase if you want a second pair of eyes on the recipes. 🤍

That would be very welcome. I want these plates to actually be used -- they'll be our main dinner service in Portugal. Twelve plates, porcelain, a simple glaze that works with food. They have to be functional above all else. I'm not going to ship twelve decorative objects across Europe. Assuming we get the glaze right in April I should have enough time to fire the full set twice before September.

Porcelain plates for daily use -- you'll want a food-safe matte, probably a cone 6 satin. I can recommend two or three options. Stoneware would be more forgiving for tableware but I assume you've considered that.

I've considered it. Stoneware is more practical but porcelain is what I want. The translucency on the rim of a thin plate when light catches it is exactly right for this project. I know it's harder. That's partly the point.
Porcelain plates hold well if the foot ring is right. Does it work as a set.

That is the question I'm trying to answer in phase one. The profile needs to be consistent across all twelve. I'm throwing to a template. Phase two is the glaze -- I'll test on off-cuts first before committing the full set. This is the most methodical approach given the timeline.

Two of them are food-safe satin cone 6 options Reuben recommended, one is a recipe Nadia found -- a matte ash variant. I have my doubts about the matte ash for tableware but I want to see how it reads on porcelain before deciding.

The satin I suggested will be more consistent for a matched set. Ash glazes have variation built in from the silica content -- on twelve identical plates you will get noticeable differences piece to piece. For functional tableware that matters.

planted_challenges.evidence_span: on twelve identical plates you will get noticeable differences piece to piece. For functional tableware that matters.

I still think the matte ash reads beautifully on porcelain though, even if it's not the practical choice here. visually it just doesn't work for me on matched tableware the way it does on a standalone piece. 🏺

I will test all three and let the results speak. If the matte ash looks right on the tile I'll reconsider. I prefer to make decisions based on evidence where possible. Assuming the tiles come out well, I'll commit the full glaze to the first three plates in the next firing.
Single glaze on a functional set is the right answer. Doesn't matter which one.
